subChunks.title: Medieval & Early Modern Genealogy (pre-1538)

storyBeats.txt: Most genealogists reach a wall at 1538, Theodora said. That is when parish registers began in England — Thomas Cromwell's order, in the name of Henry VIII. Before that date, the evidence changes completely.

The illusion that ordinary people left no records before 1538 is wrong. They left extraordinary records — just not the records we're used to. Tax lists. Manorial court rolls. Subsidy rolls. Inquisitions post mortem. Feet of fines. The records exist. You need different skills to read them.

The further back you go, the more likely you are to be tracing the privileged. The 14th century leaves fine records for landholders and virtually none for unfree peasants. But 'virtually none' is not 'absolutely none'. And with DNA, even that boundary is dissolving.

subChunks.hookHtml:
1538 is one of genealogy's most significant dates. In that year, Thomas Cromwell ordered every parish priest in England to keep a register of baptisms, marriages, and burials — the foundation of parochial registration that would run, with varying quality, until civil registration began in 1837.

Before 1538, ordinary people's births, marriages, and deaths were largely unrecorded in any systematic way. But the absence of parish records does not mean the absence of all records. Medieval England generated enormous quantities of administrative documentation — taxation, litigation, land transactions, feudal obligations, ecclesiastical proceedings — and a significant proportion of those records survive in archives and in print. Working in this period requires palaeographic skill, knowledge of Latin, and familiarity with a completely different documentary landscape.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Documentary Record Before 1538

For people who held land, paid taxes, or appeared before courts, the pre-1538 record is surprisingly rich. Key record types include:

Manorial court rolls: Manor courts (courts baron and courts leet) recorded admissions of new tenants, surrenders of land, deaths of tenants, heriot payments (a death duty), and fines for offences. Rolls survive from the 13th century for some manors and provide a continuous record of tenure for specific properties and families. Held variously at TNA (particularly for royal manors), county record offices, and private archives. The Manorial Documents Register (MDR) at TNA records where rolls for each manor are held.

Subsidy rolls and tax records: The lay subsidies of 1290, 1327, and 1332 listed taxpayers by vill (township) with amounts paid. The 1377 Poll Tax listed every person over 14. The Hearth Tax (1662–1689) listed every householder and whether they were exempt. These are invaluable name lists for specific places and periods.

Inquisitions post mortem (IPMs): When a Crown tenant died, an inquiry was held to establish who his heirs were and what lands he held. The resulting record names the deceased, their children, the extent of their lands, and often collateral relatives. Indexed and printed by the Record Commissioners; many available via British History Online (british-history.ac.uk).

Feet of fines: Legal agreements recording property transactions, entered as three-part indentures ('chirographs'). The bottom portion ('foot') was retained by the court; the other two went to the parties. Extensive feet of fines survive at TNA and at county record offices. Published indexes cover many counties.

Patent Rolls and Close Rolls: Enrolled records of royal government — grants, letters, orders. Widely printed by the Record Commission and available via British History Online.

Ecclesiastical records: Episcopal registers, visitation records, probate records (from ecclesiastical courts before 1858 in England), and chapter records. Bishops' registers survive for most English dioceses from the 13th century and record ordinations, institutions to parishes, and significant legal matters. Probate records (wills, inventories, administrations) survive from the 14th century for some courts.

Latin in Medieval Records

Almost all pre-1538 official records are in Latin (with some exceptions: English appears in some later medieval documents, and legal French is used in some court records). Effective research requires at least a working knowledge of medieval Latin — particularly the formulaic phrases used in administrative documents, which are far less daunting than classical Latin once their conventions are understood.

Resources: Latin for Local and Family Historians (Denis Stuart); A Latin Glossary for Family and Local Historians (Janet Morris, FFHS); English Latin Translator online tool (British History Online provides Latin-English glossaries for specific record types).

Palaeography Before 1538

Pre-1538 handwriting uses Secretary Hand (from the 15th century) and earlier hands — Court Hand, Chancery Hand, Textura. These differ substantially from the post-1600 Secretary Hand that genealogists typically learn first. The National Archives' online palaeography tutorials cover medieval hands, and the English Handwriting Online site (University of Cambridge) provides exercises in period-specific scripts.

Connecting to the Post-1538 Record

The practical challenge for most genealogists is bridging from the earliest traceable post-1538 ancestor into pre-1538 records. This requires: identifying the manor on which the family held land (manorial records then provide continuity); finding the family in lay subsidy rolls for the relevant township; and researching any probate records from the 1520s–1540s (some church courts had testamentary jurisdiction before 1538 and their records survive).

For gentry families, the Visitations of the Heralds (College of Arms, 1530s–1680s) recorded claimed pedigrees — an invaluable starting point for medieval connections, though the claims must be verified against original records.

DNA and Pre-1538 Research

Y-DNA testing for specific surname lineages, combined with the manorial record of family tenure, can extend a documented line backwards by identifying which Y-DNA haplogroup is consistent with documented medieval examples. This is an emerging area, particularly for families with long-documented manorial associations.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how a historian or genealogist can trace an ordinary English family back before 1538, when parish registers didn't exist, using other kinds of historical records.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: You are trying to trace the Sutton family of Sutton, Cheshire, before 1538. You know from post-1538 records that they held a small landholding in Sutton township under a local manor. What records would you search to find them in the period 1400–1538, where those records would be held, and what specific information might each record type provide?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
For a landowning family in Cheshire in 1400–1538, the following record types are most likely to yield evidence:

Manorial court rolls: Identify the manor holding jurisdiction over Sutton township — likely one of the Cheshire manors. Search the Manorial Documents Register (TNA online) to find where the rolls for that specific manor are held (may be TNA, Cheshire Archives, or a private collection). Court rolls may record admissions of Sutton family members as new tenants, their deaths, and heriots paid on death — providing approximate dates and family relationships.

Lay Subsidy rolls (1327, 1332): Earlier than the target range but may establish the family in the township. Available at TNA (E 179 series); many published by the Pipe Roll Society or county record societies. May list family members as taxpayers with amounts.

Cheshire Plea Rolls: Cheshire was a county palatine with its own legal system. Plea rolls for Chester (held at TNA, CHES series) record civil litigation and may name the Sutton family as parties.

Inquisitions Post Mortem: If the family held land from the Earl of Chester or other Crown mesne lords, an IPM may have been taken on a family member's death. Search the TNA calendar of IPMs (printed by Record Commission, also via British History Online) for Cheshire entries.

Probate records: The Chester diocese ecclesiastical courts had probate jurisdiction. Pre-1538 wills for Cheshire are held at Cheshire Archives; some are published by the Record Society of Lancashire and Cheshire.

Heralds' Visitations: If the family claimed gentry status by the 16th century, the 1580 or 1613 Cheshire Visitation may record a pedigree extending to the pre-1538 period.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Discuss the methodological challenges facing a genealogist attempting to trace a non-gentry, non-landowning family (agricultural labourers or cottagers) in England before 1538. What records might document such people? What are the significant gaps? How might DNA testing complement the limited documentary evidence? What ethical considerations apply to making confident genealogical claims about individuals this far back?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Non-gentry families before 1538 are documented far more sparsely than landholders, and the research is correspondingly more challenging.

Possible records: Poll Tax (1377) was theoretically universal for persons over 14, though evasion was common; villeins and cottagers appear in manorial court rolls as defendants in petty disputes, as witnesses, and occasionally as participants in land transactions. Some churchwardens' accounts (from the late 14th century) name parishioners contributing to church expenses. Coroners' inquests (where a suspicious death occurred) name witnesses and victims from all social levels. Guild records in towns may name craftsmen. Subsidy rolls exempt the very poor and do not provide universal coverage, but those just above the poverty line appear.

Significant gaps: births, marriages, and deaths of unfree peasants were simply not systematically recorded before 1538. A family might leave no documentary trace whatsoever for two or three generations, then reappear in a manorial court roll as a dispute over a pig.

DNA: Y-DNA surname testing can establish that a cluster of same-surname men share a common patrilineal ancestor — providing a genetic genealogical fact even where the documentary record is empty. This does not tell us who that ancestor was or when he lived, but it can confirm or refute oral traditions of common descent.

Ethical considerations: Genealogical claims for non-gentry medieval families must be stated with extreme caution. Connecting a modern family to a medieval one of the same name without documentary continuity (a traceable landholding, manorial tenure, or probate record chain) is speculative at best and misleading at worst. The temptation to 'fill in' an unrecorded gap with a plausible but unproven individual should be firmly resisted. Where the record is absent, the honest conclusion is that the ancestry cannot be documented, not that it did not exist.
learningObjectives: Identify the principal record types available for pre-1538 genealogical research in England.
Explain the role of manorial court rolls, subsidy rolls, inquisitions post mortem, and feet of fines as genealogical sources.
Describe the palaeographic and linguistic challenges of medieval records.
Evaluate the methodological limitations of pre-1538 research for non-gentry families.
commonMistakes: Assuming no records exist before 1538 — a wide range of administrative, ecclesiastical, and legal records predates parish registers.
Connecting a post-1538 family to a medieval family of the same name without a continuous documented chain of tenure or evidence.
Attempting to read medieval documents without first learning the appropriate hand — misreading Latin abbreviations and contractions leads to transcription errors.
Treating heraldic visitation pedigrees as verified fact rather than as claimed lineages requiring corroboration from original records.
assessmentCriteria: Identifies at least four distinct pre-1538 record types and explains what genealogical information each can provide.
Accurately distinguishes gentry from non-gentry record survival and explains the implications for research strategy.
Demonstrates understanding of the Manorial Documents Register as a tool for locating court roll archives.
Shows awareness of the ethical need for caution in making genealogical claims based on sparse pre-1538 evidence.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: TNA's online register recording where manorial court rolls and related records are held for each manor in England and Wales — the essential starting point for locating surviving court roll series.
Crown inquiries on the death of a tenant-in-chief establishing heirs and land held; naming the deceased, children, and often collateral family — indexed and calendared in British History Online.
Medieval property transaction records entered as tripartite indentures; the court's copy (the 'foot') survives in large quantities and provides evidence of land transfer and parties involved.
Medieval taxation records listing taxpaying householders by vill; the 1327 and 1332 rolls are particularly well-preserved and widely published, providing the earliest name lists for many townships.
Surveys by the College of Arms heralds (1530s–1680s) recording gentry pedigrees; an invaluable starting point for pre-1538 gentry connections, though claims require verification.
Tax on every person over 14 in England — theoretically universal, providing the most comprehensive pre-1538 name list for many townships, though evasion was widespread.

questions.questionHtml: What was the Manorial Documents Register (MDR) and why is it useful for pre-1538 genealogy?
options: An index of all surviving medieval baptism records held at county record offices
A register held at TNA recording where surviving manorial court rolls are held for each manor in England and Wales
A published calendar of inquisitions post mortem from 1300 to 1550
A database of medieval testators whose wills were proved before 1538
questions.correctAnswer: A register held at TNA recording where surviving manorial court rolls are held for each manor in England and Wales
questions.explanationHtml: The MDR is the essential tool for locating manorial court rolls, which are the primary pre-1538 record for tenant families. It records which archive (TNA, county record office, university library, private collection) holds the rolls for each specific manor.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher's post-1538 family held land in a Shropshire township under a local manor. To trace them before 1538, which records should be searched first?
options: The 1538 parish registers for the township
The Manorial Documents Register to identify surviving court rolls for the relevant manor, and the lay subsidy rolls for Shropshire
The Army Lists and Muster Rolls for Shropshire
questions.correctAnswer: The Manorial Documents Register to identify surviving court rolls for the relevant manor, and the lay subsidy rolls for Shropshire
questions.explanationHtml: For a landowning family before 1538, manorial court rolls (recording admissions, deaths, and land transactions) and lay subsidy rolls (listing taxpayers by township) are the most likely sources to yield the family name in a pre-1538 context.

questions.questionHtml: A genealogist claims descent from a 14th-century knight based on finding the same surname in a medieval subsidy roll for the same county. What is the fundamental problem with this claim?
options: Subsidy rolls are not admissible evidence in genealogical research
A shared surname in the same county, without a continuous documented chain linking the medieval taxpayer to the modern researcher's ancestor, is insufficient to establish descent
The claim is sound, since surnames were rarely shared in medieval England
Medieval surnames were always inherited through the female line
questions.correctAnswer: A shared surname in the same county, without a continuous documented chain linking the medieval taxpayer to the modern researcher's ancestor, is insufficient to establish descent
questions.explanationHtml: Many people of the same surname may have lived in the same county without being related. A genealogical claim requires a continuous documented chain linking the medieval individual to the later family — not just a name match. In the absence of manorial tenure records, probate records, or another continuous source tracing the family across the gap, the claim is speculative.
